hook_text: Every trig formula you'll learn this year is hiding in one spinning wheel.
clip_script: Picture a Ferris wheel from the side, one arm painted yellow, turning anticlockwise from three o'clock. Wherever that arm points, it throws two shadows: one east-west, one north-south. The east-west shadow is cosine. The north-south shadow is sine. Tangent? One shadow divided by the other. That's the whole toolkit. Now swing the arm to two hundred and ten degrees — down into the south-west. The north-south shadow points south: sine is negative. The east-west shadow points west: cosine is negative. The signs in trig are not rules to memorise. They're compass directions. Want the famous identity? The two shadows are the short sides of a right-angled triangle, and the arm is the hypotenuse. Pythagoras: shadows squared add up to the arm squared. Make the arm length one and it reads sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. That's not a formula — that's Pythagoras riding the wheel. And big angles? Every one is an acute angle in a costume. Fold the wheel along the vertical line and one hundred and fifty degrees lands right on thirty. Same size ratios, only the east-west signs flip. Find the home angle, check the quarter, write the sign. The wheel does the rest.
visual_style: A side-on Ferris wheel with one glowing yellow arm sweeping anticlockwise, dropping bright shadow bars onto a horizontal and a vertical axis, compass letters N-S-E-W pulsing, then the wheel folding like paper along the vertical line.
mood: Wonder and click-moments — the topic assembling itself from one picture.
pacing: Smooth sweeps with the wheel, a hard stop on each sign reveal, quick fold at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read every angle straight off the wheel.
